chunks: N-channel vs P-channel MOSFET. The question: What is the difference between an N-channel and P-channel?
N-channel and P-channel MOSFETs are the two mirror-image types of the same switch.
In an N-channel device the conducting path is made of electrons, and in a P-channel device it is made of holes.
Each one turns on with the opposite gate voltage, and each one likes to sit on the opposite side of a load.
Think of right-handed and left-handed scissors. They do the same job, but everything about how you hold them is mirrored.
Push the N-channel gate up above its source and it turns on. Pull the P-channel gate down below its source and it turns on.
Unlike scissors, the pair are not equally good: electrons move more easily than holes, so the N-channel one carries more current for the same size.
The NMOS sits between the load and ground (source at the low side); the PMOS sits between VDD and the load (source at the high side).
Each wants its source at its respective rail so the gate-source voltage is easy to generate from logic levels.
N-channel (NMOS): a MOSFET whose channel carries electrons. Source usually at ground. P-channel (PMOS): a MOSFET whose channel carries holes. Source usually at the supply.
Hole: a missing electron in silicon that acts like a positive charge carrier. Mobility: how easily a carrier moves. Electrons are about 2 to 3 times more mobile than holes.
Threshold ( V t ): the gate-to-source voltage that turns the device on.
Run both from a 5 volts supply. An NMOS has its source on ground, so a gate at 5 volts gives V GS equals plus 5 volts and it turns on.
A PMOS has its source on 5 volts, so a gate at 0 volts gives V GS equals -5 volts and it turns on, while a gate at 5 volts gives V GS equals 0 and it stays off.
At equal size, if the NMOS carries 2. 5 milliamps, the PMOS carries about 1 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"The difference is the carrier in the channel.
An N-channel FET has an electron channel in a p-type body, turns on with the gate above the source by more than Vt, and its source usually sits at ground.
A P-channel FET is the mirror image: hole channel, gate must go below the source, source usually at the supply.

Because holes are about 2 to 3 times less mobile than electrons, a PMOS needs to be 2 to 3 times wider to match an NMOS, so NMOS is the default and PMOS is used where it simplifies high-side drive or for the pull-up in CMOS."
